# Krunalkumar Shah

> Independent consultant specializing in cybersecurity, automation, and AI workflows. Published Linux security researcher and technical mentor. Micro enterprise registered with MSME, Govt. of India (UDYAM-GJ-23-0050928).

## Summary

- [Home](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/): Profile summary, core technical domains, credential highlights, and selected open-source builds.
- [About](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/about): Education (M.E. IT / Information Security, B.E. Computer Engineering), international career across 4 countries (India, USA, France, Taiwan), skill matrix, and community roles.
- [Services](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/services): Scoped consulting offerings: AI workflow automation (n8n, Make, HubSpot), full-stack development, Linux/web cybersecurity hardening, personal malware/account recovery, corporate and team training, and technical writing.
- [Projects](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/projects): Complete index of 35+ production automation and AI repositories (ChurnGPT 2.0, FNOL Claims Assistant, CleverResponder, HubSpot integrations).
- [Research](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/research): Academic paper "Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems" (IJRAT 2019, DOI: 10.32622/ijrat.74201911) detailing process resource quarantine mechanisms.
- [Blog](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog): Index of all published articles on cybersecurity, AI automation, and engineering practice.

## Technical Articles

- [Types of Cyberattacks, Mapped](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/types-of-cyberattacks): Technical breakdown of 6 attack vectors mapped against CIA Triad vulnerabilities and mitigation steps.
- [Security Compliance, Explained](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/security-compliance-explained): Practical enterprise guide to GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX, ISO 27001, and SOC 2 frameworks.
- [India's IT Law, Explained](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/india-it-act-explained): Legal analysis of the IT Act 2000, intermediary guidelines, CERT-In directions, and DPDP Act 2023.
- [How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/how-cybercrime-cases-are-solved): Incident response lifecycle, forensic disk/memory acquisition, chain of custody, and courtroom evidence standards.
- [Which AI Tool for Which Job](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/which-ai-tool-for-which-job): Benchmark matrix comparing AI assistants across research, coding, slides, and workflow integration.
- [I Open-Sourced My AI SDR](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/i-open-sourced-my-ai-sdr): CleverResponder architecture for inbound reply handling via SmartLead and Instantly.
- [What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux?](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/what-is-a-fork-bomb): Bash process exhaustion analysis, ulimit edge cases, and dynamic process quarantine solutions.
- [Automating Email Replies with n8n](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/automating-email-replies-with-n8n): 5-stage automated architecture: trigger, parsing, classification, draft generation, and human-in-the-loop Slack actions.
- [How to Succeed in Software Development](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/blog/how-to-succeed-in-software-development): Build order for software and automations — make it work, make it modular, make it readable, then optimize.

## Labs — free online compilers that run in the browser

- [Labs hub](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs): Five language playgrounds and a real Linux terminal, all executing locally in the visitor's browser. No server, no sign-up, nothing uploaded.
- [Online Python compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/python): Genuine CPython on WebAssembly with the standard library and input() support. No pip.
- [Online JavaScript compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/javascript): Runs on the browser's own engine in an isolated Web Worker. Nothing to download.
- [Online TypeScript compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/typescript): The official tsc, doing real type checking before anything runs.
- [Online SQL compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/sql): A real SQLite engine in memory, with results rendered as a table.
- [Online Lua compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/lua): Lua 5.4 on WebAssembly, with metatables and coroutines.
- [Online Linux terminal](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/linux): A genuine Linux kernel and BusyBox shell booted in the browser via x86 emulation. No network, safe to break.
- [Online C compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/c): A real clang and lld toolchain in the browser. structs, pointers, malloc, scanf.
- [Online C++ compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cpp): Real clang with libc++ and the full STL: vector, string, map, algorithm, templates.
- [Online PHP compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/php): Real PHP 8.4 with enums, match and the full array library.
- [Online Ruby compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/ruby): Real CRuby from the Ruby core team. Blocks, mixins, enumerables.
- [Online PostgreSQL compiler](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/postgres): The actual Postgres server with window functions, CTEs and JSONB.
- [Online DOS prompt](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/dos): Real FreeDOS booted in the browser. DIR, COPY, batch files, VIM and NASM.
- [Typing speed test for programmers](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/typing): Measured on real code, not just prose. WPM and accuracy, nothing uploaded.


## Security & digital forensics tools — all client-side

- [Hash generator & verifier](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/hash): MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 and HMAC for text or files, plus checksum verification and hash identification.
- [File type inspector & hex viewer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/file-inspector): Identifies a file from its magic bytes rather than its extension, and flags the mismatch. Hex dump, printable strings and an entropy graph.
- [JWT decoder & verifier](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/jwt): Decodes a JSON Web Token, explains every claim, checks expiry and verifies HMAC signatures. The token is never transmitted.
- [EXIF viewer & metadata remover](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/exif): Reads the camera, timestamp, serial number and GPS coordinates inside a photo, then re-encodes a stripped copy.
- [Email header analyzer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/email-headers): Parses the Received chain, reads SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, detects Reply-To spoofing and extracts the originating IP.
- [URL & phishing link inspector](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/url-inspector): Takes a suspicious link apart without ever requesting it: homograph characters, buried domains, nested encoding, open redirects.
- [Password strength checker & generator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/password): Real entropy plus offline crack times against MD5, SHA-256, bcrypt and Argon2id. Generator uses crypto.getRandomValues.
- [SSL/TLS certificate decoder](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cert-decoder): Decodes an X.509 PEM without OpenSSL: subject, issuer, validity, key size, SANs, extensions and fingerprints.
- [Certificate builder](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/certificate-forge): The certificate decoder in reverse. Generates a real RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256 keypair with WebCrypto, then hand-encodes a self-signed X.509 certificate, a PKCS#10 CSR and a two-certificate chain of trust, with the ASN.1/DER shown byte by byte and the output verified against a real X.509 parser. Also signs messages and demonstrates tamper detection. Entirely client-side.
- [Encoder & decoder](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/encoding): Base64, Base64url, Base32, Base58, hex, URL, HTML entities, binary, decimal, Morse and JSON, with automatic format detection.
- [Classical cipher playground](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cipher): Caesar, ROT13, Atbash, Vigenere and XOR — and automatic cryptanalysis that breaks all of them without a key.
- [Image steganography](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/steganography): Hides a message in the least significant bits of a PNG, extracts one, and amplifies the low-bit plane to reveal concealed data.
- [Regex tester & ReDoS checker](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/regex): Live matching with capture groups, plus an empirical catastrophic-backtracking test and a library of security-relevant patterns.
- [CVSS v3.1 calculator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cvss): The official base score formula with every metric explained and its contribution shown. Parses and emits vector strings.
- [Subnet & CIDR calculator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/subnet): IPv4 ranges, masks in every notation, the binary breakdown, and RFC 1918 / CGNAT / reserved-range classification.
- [Forensic timestamp converter](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/timestamp): Reads a value under Unix, Windows FILETIME, WebKit, Apple Cocoa, HFS+ and MS-DOS epochs at once to identify which system wrote it.

Nothing in this section uploads anything. There is no server behind these tools: evidence files, tokens, passwords and email headers are processed in the visitor's own browser tab, which is the reason they exist.


## Digital forensics tools — drop a file, all client-side

- [HAR analyzer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/har-analyzer): Find the secrets in a browser network export - tokens, cookies, keys, PII - and download a redacted copy safe to share.
- [SQLite browser](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/sqlite-browser): Open any SQLite database - Chrome history, WhatsApp, app data - browse tables, run SQL, timestamps decoded.
- [Archive inspector](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/archive-inspector): Inspect a ZIP without extracting it: zip-slip paths, zip bombs, encrypted entries and disguised executables.
- [PCAP analyzer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/pcap-analyzer): Read a packet capture: top talkers, protocols, DNS and HTTP, and plaintext credentials from unencrypted traffic.
- [Memory dump extractor](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/memory-strings): Pull strings (ASCII and UTF-16), URLs, keys, crypto addresses and embedded files out of a memory dump.
- [Registry hive parser](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/registry-viewer): Parse a Windows registry hive for autostart keys, USB history and recent activity. No Windows required.

## Interactive visualisers — canvas and WebGL, in the browser

- [Live hash cracking](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/hash-cracker): Watch a weak password hash fall in real time, with the guesses-per-second counter ticking. Off the main thread.
- [Algorithm visualizer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/algorithm-visualizer): Sorting and pathfinding, animated and steppable. See why O(n log n) beats O(n2) instead of being told.
- [CPU simulator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cpu-simulator): Write assembly and step through it one instruction at a time, watching registers, flags, stack and memory change.
- [Shader playground](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/shader-playground): Write a GLSL fragment shader and see it render live on your GPU. Time and mouse uniforms, errors with line numbers.
- [Inside a processor](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/processor-explorer): Semantic-zoom journey from chip package to die to core pipeline to logic gate to a single transistor, with animated data flow at every level. Canvas 2D, entirely client-side.
- [Word cloud generator](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/word-cloud): A free word cloud generator: paste text and the most frequent words are sized biggest and spiral-packed into shape masks (heart, star, circle, diamond, cloud), with colour palettes and font choices, downloadable as a PNG. Filler words are removed automatically. Everything runs in the browser with no upload and no watermark; a wordart.com-style tool made free and private.
- [TCP](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/tcp-congestion): TCP made watchable in three families: the three-way handshake and four-way close with real sequence and acknowledgement arithmetic, the TCP state machine walked by both endpoints, and TCP Reno congestion control simulated round trip by round trip — slow start, congestion avoidance, fast recovery on triple-duplicate ACKs and collapse to one on a timeout, plotted as the classic sawtooth. A live simulation checked against RFC 793 examples, entirely client-side.
- [Buffer overflow](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/buffer-overflow): A stack buffer overflow drawn byte by byte on a real downward-growing stack: watch a string copy overwrite the saved frame pointer and the return address, hijack control flow to injected shellcode (as a diagram, never executed), then enable a stack canary and watch it catch the overflow. A defences panel shows what NX and ASLR each stop and how each is bypassed. Entirely client-side, a teaching diagram for defenders.
- [Regex engine](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/regex-engine): A regular expression engine built from scratch: recursive descent parser, Thompson NFA construction, subset construction to a DFA, and a backtracking matcher, all steppable. The ReDoS panel measures backtracking cost against input length and compares it with the linear-time state-machine engines. All three engines are differentially tested against JavaScript RegExp. Entirely client-side.
- [Cryptography](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/cryptography): AES-128 stepped through all 40 transformations with a live avalanche measurement, SHA-256 across its 64 compression rounds, and Diffie-Hellman, RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange with small checkable numbers plus a working brute-force attacker. Teaching implementations, verified against FIPS-197 and FIPS-180-4 test vectors. Entirely client-side.
- [OS algorithms](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/os-algorithms): CPU scheduling (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, round robin, priority), page replacement (FIFO, LRU, OPT, clock, LFU), disk scheduling (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK), memory allocation (first/best/worst/next fit) and the Banker safety check, stepped through one unit of time at a time with every algorithm compared side by side. Entirely client-side.
- [Fractal explorer](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/fractal-explorer): Zoom the Mandelbrot and Julia sets smoothly on your GPU. Hover to pick a Julia constant.

## HackLab — a deliberately vulnerable app for learning offensive security

- [HackLab](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/hacklab): Break real vulnerabilities in your browser — SQL injection against a live SQLite engine, reflected XSS in a sandboxed opaque-origin frame, path traversal, command injection and IDOR. Every target is a throwaway in-memory fake; nothing is uploaded and there is no server to attack. Each challenge pairs the exploit with its real-world fix.

## Network lookup tools — these DO make requests

- [DNS lookup](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/dns): A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, SOA and CAA over DNS-over-HTTPS, with your choice of resolver. A browser cannot speak DNS directly - this is how it gets there. Queries Google or Cloudflare directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Email security audit](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/email-security): Can somebody send mail pretending to be this domain? SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS and BIMI, parsed and graded, from public DNS alone. Queries Google Public DNS directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Certificate transparency](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/ct-log): Every certificate ever logged for a domain, and the subdomains printed on them - discovered without sending a single packet to the target. Queries SSLMate Cert Spotter directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Domain registration (RDAP)](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/rdap): Registration date, expiry, transfer locks and DNSSEC. Classic WHOIS needs a raw TCP socket; RDAP speaks HTTPS, so there is no proxy in the path. Queries the authoritative registry directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.
- [Password breach check](https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/labs/breach-check): Is this password in a known breach? Only five characters of its hash are sent, and the comparison happens in your tab. k-anonymity, not a promise. Queries Have I Been Pwned directly from the visitor's browser; no proxy.

These are deliberately separated from the fifteen offline security tools. They still use no proxy — the visitor's browser contacts the vendor directly — but unlike the rest of Labs, a request genuinely leaves the machine, and each page says which vendor and what they learn before anything fires.
